strengths: The motivation is clear and well-reasoned: moving from a single static LoRA or computationally expensive hypernetworks/test-time optimization to a jointly trained basis of LoRAs with a dynamic weighting router is an elegant solution for spanning diverse visual transformation spaces.
The architectural design effectively combines the high-level semantic gating of CLIP/SigLIP with the detailed in-context generative capabilities of modern diffusion transformers (Flux.1-Kontext).

The evaluation methodology is thorough, combining traditional metrics (LPIPS, CLIP directional similarity) with modern VLM-based pairwise preference protocols (Gemma-3) and a validated human user study, showing consistent preference for LoRWeB.

The paper provides insightful ablations covering basis capacity (trade-offs between rank $r$ and basis count $N$), routing activations (Softmax vs. Tanh), input layouts for the conditioning encoder, and alternate vision backbones.
weaknesses: The performance improvement over the capacity-matched single LoRA baseline ($r=128$) is relatively moderate (e.g., win rate of 57.6% in the user study, and fairly close automated metrics in Tab. 1 / Tab. S2), whereas the largest margins are primarily against earlier diffusion backbones.

The reliance on text prompts: although visual analogy is meant to convey transformations difficult to describe textually, the method still utilizes guiding text prompts. While Figure 7 tests prompt invariance to different exemplars, the manuscript lacks an evaluation of the system in a strictly prompt-free setting (or with generic prompts like 'apply the transformation').
Minor editorial oversights: several typos exist in figures and captions, e.g., 'appraoch' (p. 3), 'RelationAadpter' in Figures 4, 7, and S2, and 'analoy' / 'LoRBA' in the caption of Figure S1.

strengths: The core idea of spanning the visual analogy transformation space via an end-to-end learnable basis of LoRAs dynamically combined through an encoder-router is well-motivated, elegant, and avoids the instability of hypernetworks and the computational cost of test-time optimization.

Comprehensive experimental validation combining standard visual metrics (LPIPS, CLIP Directional), detailed VLM-based evaluations (Gemma-3), and a human perceptual user study showing consistent improvements over single-adapter and prior state-of-the-art baselines.

Insightful ablations covering critical architectural choices, including the trade-off between basis size ($N$) and rank ($r$), normalization functions (Softmax vs. Tanh), encoder inputs, and backbone encoders.
Figure 7 provides a compelling qualitative demonstration that the model truly respects visual nuances from the analogy pair $\{a, a'\}$ rather than purely relying on the text prompt.
weaknesses: The pipeline still relies on a guiding text edit prompt alongside the visual analogy triplet. A more extensive quantitative evaluation assessing performance under neutral, generic, or completely missing prompts would strengthen the claim of pure visual analogy learning.

The paper lacks an analysis of the computational and inference latency overhead incurred by dynamically computing and merging the LoRA weights for each target layer on the fly compared to a standard single LoRA.

An interpretability analysis of the learned basis (e.g., visualizing what individual basis components capture, or visualizing routing weight distributions across different categories of transformations) is missing and would provide valuable insight into how the basis spans the transformation space.
Minor typographic errors exist in figures and captions (e.g., 'Relation Aadpter' in Fig. 4 and Fig. S2, and 'LoRBA' in the caption of Fig. S1).

strengths: The core idea of replacing a single static LoRA with an end-to-end learnable basis of low-rank adapters and a dynamic routing mechanism for visual analogy completion is well-motivated and structurally sound.

Unlike test-time optimization approaches that require expensive per-instance fitting, LoRWeB predicts linear combination coefficients in a single forward pass, collapsing the mixed LoRA into a single set of weights prior to denoising, which incurs virtually zero additional compute overhead during inference.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, combining standard similarity metrics (LPIPS, CLIP Directional), a detailed VLM-based protocol (Gemma-3), and a 2AFC human user study with inter-annotator/VLM alignment analysis.

The paper includes solid ablations examining critical architectural choices, including basis rank versus count, normalization functions, encoder architectures (CLIP vs. SigLIP2), and image input formatting.
weaknesses: The quantitative margin over the parameter-matched single LoRA baseline (r=128) is relatively modest (e.g., 57.6% user preference win rate and a small shift along the Pareto frontier in Table S2 / Figure 5), indicating that the single high-rank LoRA remains quite competitive.

A key motivation for visual analogy learning is enabling image manipulation when transformations cannot easily be articulated via language. However, LoRWeB heavily relies on explicit text prompts as input alongside the image context grid; evaluating the model under prompt-free or ambiguous-prompt settings would better establish the necessity of the visual analogy routing mechanism.
The evaluation relies heavily on synthetic validation pairs generated by querying foundation models and community LoRAs rather than real-world paired manipulation datasets.
Several noticeable typographical errors detract from the presentation quality (e.g., 'Our appraoch' in Section 3.2, 'RelationAadpter' in Figures 4, 7, and S2, and 'LoRBA' in the Figure S1 caption).

strengths: The proposed dynamic LoRA weight basis formulation effectively addresses the expressive bottleneck of single-adapter visual analogy methods without requiring costly per-sample optimization at test time.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrates consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements over relevant baselines, supported by human user studies and VLM-based evaluations.
The paper provides informative ablations exploring key design dimensions, including basis size, rank trade-offs, routing activation functions, and encoder inputs.
weaknesses: The method still relies on accompanying text prompt guidance alongside exemplar pairs, leaving the capability of pure visual-only analogy learning somewhat constrained.
The paper lacks in-depth analysis or interpretability regarding the learned basis LoRAs, leaving it unclear whether distinct semantic transformation primitives are actually disentangled.
The framework struggles with fine-grained visual transformations and multi-attribute modifications, partly due to resolution bottlenecks in the CLIP encoding stage.

strengths: Formulates visual analogy learning via a dynamic linear combination of a learned LoRA basis, avoiding test-time optimization while retaining single-pass efficiency.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple metrics (VLM-based evaluation, human user study, and CLIP directional similarity) demonstrating consistent improvements over single-adapter and prior analogy baselines.
Thorough ablation study analyzing basis capacity, rank trade-offs, routing activation functions, and encoder architectures.
weaknesses: The framework still partially relies on textual edit prompts alongside the image exemplar pair, making it not entirely driven by visual demonstration alone.
Performance degrades when exemplar pairs require subtle, fine-grained edits or contain complex multi-part modifications, partly constrained by CLIP image resolution.
Assumes access to cleanly isolated reference transformations where extraneous background and identity variations are minimal.

strengths: Learning a dynamic basis of LoRAs offers an effective trade-off between the rigidity of a single static adapter and the heavy computational expense of test-time optimization.
The proposed routing mechanism incurs negligible inference overhead (+3.1% runtime) while yielding substantial empirical gains over single-adapter baselines.
Comprehensive evaluation combining automated VLM ratings, standard perceptual metrics, user studies, and systematic ablations.
weaknesses: The framework remains partially dependent on text prompts, somewhat compromising the core premise of pure demonstration-based visual analogies.
Routing relies on a downsampled CLIP encoder (224x224), which struggles to capture fine-grained or localized structural modifications between exemplar pairs.
Analysis of the learned basis is limited, leaving open questions regarding basis orthogonality, redundancy, and semantic specialization across adapters.
